title: Subgroups and the One-Step Test
quickIdea: A subgroup is a subset that is a group under the same operation. The one-step test, a b^-1 in H for all a and b in H, settles it in a single line.
remember: H is a subgroup of G when H is a non-empty subset and is itself a group under the operation of G; associativity is inherited and never rechecked.
One-step test: non-empty H is a subgroup if and only if a b^-1 is in H for every a, b in H. Additively, a - b in H. Two-step version: a b in H and a^-1 in H.
Every subgroup contains the identity; {e} and G are the trivial subgroups; any other is proper, and |H| = 1 forces H = {e}.
The intersection of any collection of subgroups is a subgroup. The union of two subgroups is a subgroup only when one of them contains the other.
For a finite group, closure alone already gives a subgroup: the powers of an element eventually repeat and the repeat supplies the inverse. For an infinite group closure is not enough.
Every subgroup of a cyclic group is cyclic, and every subgroup of an abelian group is abelian.
The order of a subgroup divides the order of the group, by Lagrange; the converse of that statement is false.

example.prompt: Which of {0, 3, 6, 9} and {0, 2, 4} are subgroups of (Z_12, +)?
example.work: In additive notation the one-step test is a - b in H. In {0, 3, 6, 9} every difference lands back in the set: 3 - 9 = -6 = 6, 9 - 3 = 6, 6 - 3 = 3, 9 - 6 = 3. So it is a subgroup of order 4. In {0, 2, 4}, the difference 2 - 4 = -2 = 10 is not in the set, and neither is the sum 4 + 4 = 8, so it is not closed.
example.answer: {0, 3, 6, 9} is a subgroup of order 4; {0, 2, 4} is not a subgroup, because it is not closed under addition.

gateAngle: Subgroup questions are decided by a counterexample or by Lagrange. If the question asks how many subgroups a small group has, list the divisors of |G| first and then test each candidate size with a - b in H.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: Is the union of two subgroups always a subgroup?
variations.answer: No: in Z_12 the union of {0, 6} and {0, 4, 8} is {0, 4, 6, 8}, and 4 + 6 = 10 is missing.
variations.why: Unions break closure; intersections never do. This is the single most common false statement about subgroups.

variations.label: ORIGINAL PYQ-STYLE QUESTION
variations.question: How many subgroups does Z_12 have?
variations.answer: Six, one for each divisor of 12: orders 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 12.
variations.why: A cyclic group has exactly one subgroup per divisor. That reverse direction is special to cyclic groups and is exactly what Lagrange does not give you in general.

variations.label: PREDICTED VARIATION
variations.question: In an abelian group, is the set of all elements of finite order a subgroup?
variations.answer: Yes. If a^m = e and b^n = e then (a b^-1)^(m n) = e, so the one-step test passes.
variations.why: The one-step test is built for closure arguments of exactly this shape, where the group is infinite and listing elements is impossible.

trap.what: Using closure as the whole subgroup test on an infinite group, or 'proving' a subgroup by checking three example pairs.
trap.why: In an infinite group closure can hold while inverses are missing, and a test is a statement about every pair, not a sample.
trap.counterexample: In (Z, +) the set {0, 1, 2, 3, ...} is closed under addition but is not a subgroup, because -1 is missing.

check.question: Show that H = {0, 4, 8} is a subgroup of Z_12 and give its index.
check.answer: Differences of elements of H stay in H, so H is a subgroup; |H| = 3 and |G| = 12, so the index is 4.
check.explanation: 0 - 4 = 8, 4 - 8 = 8, 8 - 0 = 8 and the like all land in {0, 4, 8}, so the one-step test passes. The index is the number of cosets, |G| / |H| = 12 / 3 = 4.
